bib.title: Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Krishna, Zhu, Groth, Johnson, Hata, Kravitz, Chen, Kalantidis, Li, Shamma, Bernstein, Fei-Fei, "Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations", Int J Comput Vis 123:32–73, 2017 (open access, CC BY 4.0).

COVERAGE: I read all 42 PDF pages, about 124K of 142K extracted chars, in full: body, every table, Sections 1–8, and the start of the references. The rest of the reference list I only skimmed. The paper has no appendices.

CLAIMS
- claim: Visual Genome's size and density. Table 1, PDF p9, lists 108,077 images, 50 descriptions per image, 3,843,636 objects across 33,877 categories (35 per image), 68,111 attribute categories (26 per image), 42,374 relationship categories (21 per image) and 1,773,258 QA pairs. Text gives 2.8M total attributes and 2,347,187 relationships. Section 6.3 counts 5,406,939 region descriptions.
  setup: First release. Category counts are taken after lower-casing and stemming the names.
  quote: "Visual Genome 108,077 50 3,843,636 33,877 35 68,111 26 42,374 21 1,773,258" (p9); "Our dataset contains 2.8 million total attributes with 68 ,111 unique attributes" (p21); "We have 5,406,939 region descriptions in total." (p36)
- claim: Every image is also a COCO image. The set is the Creative Commons intersection of MS-COCO and YFCC100M, so it overlaps COCO completely. The images are skewed toward people and sports.
  setup: Flickr photos, non-iconic, 72–1280 px wide (mean width 500).
  quote: "all 108 ,077 creative commons images from the intersection of MS-COCO's ( Lin et al. 2014 ) 328 , 000 images and YFCC100M's" (p16); "we have twice as many annotations for men than we do of women" (p21)
- claim: Collection pipeline. Workers wrote region descriptions as boxes plus phrases, up to 50 per image. A BLEU threshold of 0.7 against earlier descriptions blocked repeats. Other workers then extracted objects and drew tight boxes (4 px tolerance), and others added attributes and relationships. Boxes with IoU 0.9 were merged into one object after a worker confirmed the match. All of it was done on AMT by more than 33,000 workers.
  setup: About 800K HITs over 6 months, after 15 months of iteration; 93.02% of workers were in the US.
  quote: "This process is repeated until we have collected 50 region descriptions for each image." (p13); "BLEU score thresholds set to 0 .7" (p13); "a total of over 33, 000 unique workers contributed" (p12)
- claim: Verification. Three workers vote on each annotation and it is kept if at least two accept it. Objects are the exception: they were checked with "rapid judgments" instead. The paper reports no inter-annotator agreement statistic such as kappa. The only measured quality figures are for WordNet canonicalization (Table 5: objects P 88.0 / R 98.5, attributes 85.7 / 95.9, relationships 92.9 / 88.5), each checked on a hand-labelled sample of 200.
  setup: The canonicalization figures come from samples of 200 hand-mapped items.
  quote: "An annotation is added to our dataset if at least two (a majority) out of the three workers verify that it is correct." (p15); "Objects 88.0 98.5" (p31)
- claim: Baselines are weak. VGG-16 fine-tuned on crops scored 18.97% top-1 on attribute prediction (top 100 attributes) and 43.17% top-1 when predicting object and attribute jointly. Predicate prediction scored 8.74% top-1, and the joint subject/relation/object task 25.83% top-1.
  setup: About 50K attribute instances, 43K object-attribute instances and 27K triples, split 80/10/10 by image.
  quote: "18 .97% top-one accuracy and 43.11% top-ﬁve accuracy" (p34); "8 .74% top-one accuracy and 29 .69% top-ﬁve accuracy" (p35)
- claim: Region captioning and QA. NeuralTalk trained on VG beat the same model trained on Flickr: crowd-judged correctness was 43.03% vs 1.6%, CIDEr 0.30 vs 0.05. On QA, simply answering with the most frequent answers covers 41.1% of test answers at top-100, against 0.966 for humans. "Why" questions reach only 3.4% at top-100. Binary yes/no questions were excluded; VQA has 38.37% of them.
  setup: Region captions were scored on ground-truth crops. QA was split 60/40 by image, and the human figure is a 10-way multiple-choice score.
  quote: "we got 1.6 and 43.03% for models trained on Flickr30K and on Visual Genome, respectively" (p36); "Overall 0.411 0.573 0.641 0.966" (p38)

LIMITS: The authors concede that annotations are not exhaustive: "it is not feasible to collect an exhaustive set of attributes and relationships for every object". Their example is a correct "white" prediction that was marked wrong (p34, p38). The image set is biased toward people and sports. Synsets are not standardized. The paper does not test grounding, phrase localization or referring expressions, and has no dense-captioning model; it lists dense captioning only as future work. Object detection and scene-graph retrieval were deliberately left out. The baselines are 2015-era models (VGG-16, NeuralTalk, frequency-based QA). The paper has no train/test benchmark split and no measure of how COCO overlap could contaminate evaluations. It reports no agreement statistic.

BUILDS ON: Johnson et al. 2015 (scene graphs for image retrieval, CVPR). Lin et al. 2014 (MS-COCO, ECCV). Thomee et al. 2016 (YFCC100M). Antol et al. 2015 (VQA, ICCV). Miller 1995 (WordNet). Snow et al. 2008 (majority voting). Krishna et al. 2016 (rapid judgments). Karpathy and Fei-Fei 2015 (NeuralTalk). Sadeghi and Farhadi 2011 (Visual Phrases). Papineni et al. 2002 (BLEU).

CODE: none.

FIGURES: Fig. 4, p6. Caption: "A representation of the Visual Genome dataset. Each image contains region descriptions that describe a localized portion of the image. We collect two types of question answer pairs (QAs): freeform QAs and region-based QAs. Each region is converted to a region graph representation of objects, attributes, and pairwise relationships. Finally, each of these region graphs are combined to form a scene graph with all the objects grounded to the image." One picture shows the region → box → graph data shape that grounding models train on. A second option is Fig. 14, p17: 50 region boxes on one image.

PROBLEMS: Some numbers in the source contradict each other.
- Table 7 gives relationship top-5 as 26.69, while the text says 29.69.
- Table 8 labels its baseline row "Flickr8K", while the text says Flickr30K.
- Description length is stated as max 12 words in the text and 16 in Fig. 16; p7 also says 16.
- Relationships per region graph are "21" in the text but 0.43 in Table 4.
- The total is written "2,347,187 million".
- Relationships per image are given as 19 in one place and 21 elsewhere.

The Fig. 30 labels came out garbled in extraction. Some font-encoding warnings appeared, but the body text read cleanly. The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
